To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
We have performed a new search for evaporating primordial black holes using 5.5 yr of archival data from an atmospheric Cerenkov telescope.

we set an upper limit on the PBH evaporations rate of 1.1 × 106 pc3 yr1 (95% CL) in the local region, and we set upper limits on the fraction Ωpbh that PBHs make up of the critical density of the Universe.

we have searched for TeV gamma rays from the evaporations of primordial black holes, and have set a limit on the PBH evaporations rate of 1.09 × 106 pc-3 yr-1, which is more than a 2 times improvement over previous limits.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the search for the evaporation of primordial black holes, which is a very promising way to test the Hawking radiation.
the study of the early universe and the search for primordial particles.
the study of the gamma-ray bursts from primordial black holes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the search for PBHs in the local region has yielded negative results.
the Whipple data do not rule out the possibility that PBHs make up a substantial fraction of the critical mass density of the universe.
no primordial black holes have been detected in our local region of the Galaxy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have improved the limits on PBH evaporation rates by more than an order of magnitude, while also providing the most stringent constraints on the fraction of PBHs in the local universe to date, in a model-independent fashion.
the Whipple telescope is not a competitive tool to probe the PBH evolutions.

the upper limit on Ωpbh is 0.0015 (99% CL), assuming a PBH evaporation time of 10−24 s and a PBH evaportion rate of 10−3 s−1, and a PBH mass of 1015 g, which is consistent with previous constraints on Ωpbh from the diffuse MeV background.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while the Whipple data do not provide evidence for the existence of PBH evaporations in the TeV range, it does not rule out the existence of PBHS with a mass of 1015 g.

the Whipple Telescope can be a very useful instrument for PBH searches, and we expect that the next-generation gamma-ray observatory, the Cherenkov Telescope Array, will be even more sensitive to PBH evaporations.

, while the Whipple data are not sensitive enough to detect PBHs in the mass range of 1015-1017 g, future experiments with much higher sensitivity will be able to detect evaporating PBHs in this mass range.
